description: Functionalist, Marxist, Weberian and feminist theories of social stratification.
content_html:
What Is Social Stratification?

Social stratification refers to the system by which society ranks categories of people in a hierarchy. In every known human society, some groups enjoy greater wealth, status and power than others. Sociologists disagree fundamentally about why this unequal ordering exists, whether it serves useful purposes, and whether it is just. This lesson examines the conflict versus consensus debate on stratification, comparing the functionalist, Marxist, Weberian and feminist positions.

Key Fact

The four main perspectives on stratification are: functionalist (stratification is a necessary and meritocratic system), Marxist (stratification serves ruling-class interests through exploitation), Weberian (stratification is three-dimensional: class, status and party) and feminist (stratification reflects patriarchal power relations as much as class or merit).

The Consensus View: Functionalism and Davis and Moore

Writing from a functionalist perspective, Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore (1945) argued that social stratification performs two essential tasks for society: effective role allocation and performance linked to rewards. Their argument runs as follows: societies contain positions that vary in their functional importance — a surgeon performs a role more critical to social survival than many others. The pool of talented individuals capable of filling such roles is limited, so society must motivate the most talented to undergo the necessary training by attaching high rewards — high pay, prestige and status — to functionally important roles.

The result, in Davis and Moore’s view, is a meritocracy — a society in which positions are filled on the basis of ability and effort, not birth. Stratification is therefore not only inevitable but socially necessary: unequal rewards are the mechanism by which societies ensure the right people end up doing the most important jobs. A key early critic was Melvin Tumin, who challenged whether “functional importance” can be measured objectively and argued that stratification may actually restrict the talent pool by creating barriers for talented individuals from lower-class backgrounds.

An open system is one in which social mobility is possible — individuals can move up or down the hierarchy through their own efforts. Contemporary societies such as the UK are described as relatively open. Davis and Moore’s model assumes an open, meritocratic system in which talent finds its reward.

A closed system is one in which social position is fixed at birth and movement is not permitted. The caste system, historically practised in parts of South Asia, is the clearest example. Critics of Davis and Moore note that the UK class system has significant closed elements: privately educated individuals are over-represented in the highest professions, suggesting ascribed status continues to shape outcomes independently of talent.

The Conflict View I: Marxist Theory of Stratification

Karl Marx offered a fundamentally different account. From a Marxist perspective, stratification is not a neutral meritocratic mechanism — it is a system that serves the interests of the bourgeoisie at the expense of the proletariat. Marx argued that in capitalist society there are essentially two classes: those who own the means of production and those who are compelled to sell their labour. The relationship between them is one of exploitation: the bourgeoisie extract surplus value from workers’ labour, paying less in wages than the value workers create.

Marx introduced the concept of false class consciousness to explain why the proletariat do not always challenge their position: the ruling class uses ruling class ideology to make exploitation appear natural and inevitable. From this view, Davis and Moore’s functionalist theory is itself a form of ruling-class ideology — it legitimises unequal rewards as though they were purely meritocratic. Marx also used the concept of socio-economic classifications, recognising that in practice class positions are more complex than a simple two-class model, though he retained the bourgeoisie–proletariat division as the fundamental driver of social change.

The Conflict View II: Weberian Theory of Stratification

Max Weber agreed with Marx that class inequality was a powerful force, but argued that stratification could not be reduced to economics alone. Weber proposed a three-dimensional model: stratification operates through class (economic position in the market), status (social prestige and honour) and party (organised power and political influence). These three dimensions are related but not identical — a person may have high economic class but low social status (a newly wealthy person excluded from established social circles), or high status but limited economic resources (a declining aristocracy).

Weber also developed the concept of social closure — the way in which high-status groups maintain their position by restricting entry. Professional bodies that control who can enter a high-status occupation are practising social closure, using credentials and networks to exclude rivals. Weber’s three-dimensional model is often seen as offering a more nuanced account of inequality than Marx’s two-class model, because it can explain forms of inequality — ethnic, religious, status-based — that are not reducible to ownership of the means of production.

Students sometimes treat stratification as purely about income. Weber’s three-dimensional model is a direct challenge to this. A person’s position in the stratification system depends on their market position (class), their social prestige (status) and their access to collective power (party). These can diverge significantly. An examiner-flagged error is to describe any high-income person as “high class” in Weber’s terms — Weber would require analysis of market position, status group membership and political influence separately. A Mastering-tier answer on a 12-mark Evaluate question will contrast the Marxist two-class economic model with the Weberian multidimensional framework.

The Conflict View III: Feminist Theory and Patriarchy

Feminist sociologists argue that both functionalist and Marxist accounts of stratification overlook the significance of gender as an independent dimension of inequality. Where Davis and Moore see reward levels as reflecting functional importance, and Marx sees them as reflecting class exploitation, feminist sociologists point out that neither adequately explains why women’s labour — both in the paid workforce and in domestic life — has historically been undervalued.

Sylvia Walby (1990) argued that patriarchy is an independent structural system that operates alongside class. Care work, nursing and teaching — predominantly female occupations — tend to be rewarded less highly than male-dominated professions requiring comparable training, not because they are less functionally important but because reward levels reflect gender power relations. Feminist sociologists also note that stratification systems have historically restricted women from access to education, professional training and political participation, regardless of their individual talent — a direct challenge to the meritocratic claims of Davis and Moore.

Key Fact

In a 12-mark Evaluate question on stratification, the highest marks come from presenting all four perspectives: functionalist (Davis and Moore — meritocratic necessity), Marxist (stratification serves ruling-class interests), Weberian (three-dimensional class–status–party model, social closure) and feminist (patriarchy as an independent system of stratification). Close with a supported judgement about which perspective offers the most convincing explanation.
exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark Evaluate question about sociological explanations of stratification, the most common error is presenting only one or two perspectives. The mark scheme rewards candidates who systematically compare the consensus view (Davis and Moore’s functionalist meritocracy) with conflict views (Marxist exploitation, Weberian three-dimensional model, feminist patriarchy). A Mastering-tier answer will name at least two contrasting perspectives with precise sociological vocabulary — bourgeoisie, proletariat, false class consciousness, social closure, patriarchy — and close with a supported judgement that weighs the evidence. Avoid the common error of treating the conflict versus consensus debate as though “one side is right” — sociology examines which perspective is more convincing given the evidence, not which is factually correct.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Davis and Moore (1945) argued from a functionalist perspective that stratification is a universal necessity: attaching high rewards to functionally important roles ensures effective role allocation and motivated performance in a meritocratic system. Critics including Tumin challenged whether functional importance is objectively measurable.
  • Marx argued that stratification serves the interests of the bourgeoisie through exploitation of the proletariat, sustained by ruling class ideology and false class consciousness. Weber modified this with a three-dimensional model (class, status, party) and the concept of social closure.
  • Feminist sociologists, especially Walby (1990), argued that patriarchy is an independent structural system of stratification that neither functionalist nor Marxist accounts adequately explain — reward levels reflect gender power relations as well as functional importance or class position.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociological perspective argues that social stratification is a universal necessity that ensures talented people fill the most important roles?
A) Marxist
B) Feminist
C) Functionalist
D) Interactionist

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that false class consciousness is a Marxist concept about working-class understanding; 1 mark for explaining that it describes a situation where the working class fails to recognise their own exploitation and accepts the existing social order as natural and inevitable. Example: 'False class consciousness is a Marxist term for the situation where members of the proletariat fail to recognise that they are being exploited by the bourgeoisie, instead accepting the unequal social order as fair or inevitable because ruling class ideology makes it appear natural.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one criticism of Davis and Moore's functionalist theory of stratification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a criticism (e.g. Tumin argued functional importance cannot be objectively measured; feminist critique that reward structures reflect gender bias; Marxist argument that stratification serves ruling-class interests). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Tumin argued that it is impossible to measure which roles are genuinely most functionally important to society. He noted that care workers and refuse collectors perform essential work yet are poorly rewarded compared with entertainers and senior executives, whose contribution to social survival is less obvious. This undermines Davis and Moore's claim that reward levels reflect functional necessity.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Weber's three-dimensional model of social stratification.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Students should include: Weber argued that stratification operates through three separate but related dimensions rather than the single economic dimension identified by Marx (1 mark); class refers to a person's market position and economic resources (1 mark); status refers to social prestige and honour, which does not always correspond to economic wealth (1 mark); party refers to organised political power and influence, giving groups the ability to pursue collective interests through action (1 mark). Any three of these points developed with an example earns full marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that social stratification benefits society as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two named perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: Davis and Moore's functionalist thesis is explained in depth — effective role allocation, performance linked to rewards, meritocracy, societal necessity. Contrasting: Marxist critique (stratification serves bourgeoisie, ruling class ideology, exploitation, false class consciousness) and/or feminist critique (patriarchy distorts reward structures independently of functional importance). Named sociologists used throughout. A supported judgement weighs the evidence and reaches a substantiated conclusion.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, clear judgement offered though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped; some named theorists; conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations of why inequality exists in modern society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments for and against a range of perspectives. Functionalist position (Davis and Moore) explained in depth: unequal rewards attached to functionally important roles, meritocracy, role allocation. At least two contrasting perspectives developed with equal depth: Marxist (bourgeoisie/proletariat relationship, exploitation, ruling class ideology, false class consciousness, two-class system); Weberian (three dimensions of class, status and party — social closure as a mechanism of exclusion beyond mere economics); feminist (Walby — patriarchy as an independent structural system, gender pay gap, historically male-defined functional importance). Named sociologists and concepts used throughout. A clear, supported judgement weighs the perspectives and reaches a substantiated conclusion about which best explains inequality in contemporary Britain.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present; both sides covered; named sociologists referenced; judgement at the end though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or two-sided but undeveloped; some named theorists; conclusion assertive rather than substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few or no named sociologists, little or no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: According to Davis and Moore, what is the main purpose of attaching high rewards to functionally important roles?
options: To reward people for their inherited class position
To ensure the bourgeoisie retain economic control
To motivate the most talented individuals to fill socially important positions
To create a rigid closed stratification system

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociologist proposed a three-dimensional model of stratification based on class, status and party?
In Marx's theory, the _____ own the means of production and exploit the labour of the proletariat.
Weber described the process by which high-status groups restrict access to their privileges as social _____.
Match each perspective to its core claim about social stratification:
right: Stratification is a meritocratic necessity ensuring talented people fill important roles
Stratification serves ruling-class interests and is sustained by ruling class ideology
Stratification reflects patriarchal power relations as well as class position

flashcard_questions.q: What did Davis and Moore argue about social stratification?
flashcard_questions.a: That it is a universal necessity ensuring talented people fill functionally important roles through unequal rewards.
A system in which social position is determined by individual talent and effort rather than inherited privilege.
The way society is divided into a hierarchy of layers, with the most privileged at the top and least privileged at the bottom.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the bourgeoisie in Marxist theory?
flashcard_questions.a: The capitalist class who own the means of production and exploit the labour of the proletariat.
When the working class fails to recognise their own exploitation, accepting inequality as natural due to ruling class ideology.

flashcard_questions.q: What are Weber's three dimensions of stratification?
flashcard_questions.a: Class (market position), status (social prestige) and party (organised political power).
The process by which groups restrict access to their privileges to their own members, excluding outsiders.
Social position determined at birth or through family background rather than personal achievement.
Social position earned through individual effort, qualifications or merit.

flashcard_questions.q: How do feminist sociologists criticise Davis and Moore's stratification theory?
flashcard_questions.a: Reward structures reflect patriarchal values, not objective functional importance, undervaluing female-dominated roles.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Tumin argue against Davis and Moore?
flashcard_questions.a: That functional importance cannot be objectively measured and stratification may restrict the talent pool rather than maximise it.

flashcard_questions.q: What is patriarchy according to Walby?
flashcard_questions.a: A structural system in which men hold dominant power across social institutions and women are systematically disadvantaged.

glossary_terms.definition: The way society is divided into a hierarchy of layers, with the most privileged at the top and the least privileged at the bottom.
A system in which social position is determined by individual talent, effort and achievement rather than inherited privilege.
In Marxist theory, the capitalist class who own the means of production and extract surplus value from workers' labour.
In Marxist theory, the working class who must sell their labour to the bourgeoisie to survive.
In Marxist theory, a situation where the working class fails to recognise their own exploitation and accepts the existing unequal order as natural.
The process by which certain groups restrict access to privileges or resources to their own members, excluding outsiders.
Social position determined at birth or through family background rather than by personal achievement.
A system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions.
